title: Can Law Firms Redesign Themselves for AI? Jen Leonard on Unprecedented — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Sharon Crane · Jen Leonard is also the subject as co-host/author

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source accepts the competence paradox and materially develops the response: AI may displace developmental work while lawyers still need judgment to supervise it, so training should be reconstructed through flexible, collaborative, experiential and simulated models. It also qualifies the cluster by questioning whether routine junior work reliably produced judgment and by treating replacement models as experiments rather than proven equivalents.
qs: But then, as everyone's talked about, how do you gain the skills and the judgment to really supervise the output?

There is such a gap, especially in the handoff between schools and employers, and especially because of the confusion that AI has created across those groups, that we really need new models — and models that are capable of being flexible.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central apprenticeship problem—lawyers must develop judgment to supervise AI even as AI absorbs traditional training work—and materially extends it with a concrete response: cross-sector collaboration and experimental, experiential and simulated learning. It presents these as proposals rather than proven solutions and acknowledges that the supervisory-judgment problem remains unresolved.

I think we're going to see, obviously, more, and we're looking to do some more experimental and experiential and simulated learning so that people can do more practice.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source accepts that AI is weakening already-fragile apprenticeship and expertise-development routes, then materially develops the cluster’s proposed response through simulated practice, flexible training models and cross-sector partnerships. It remains appropriately conditional about whether simulation can produce the judgment needed to supervise AI.
qs: There is such a gap, especially in the handoff between schools and employers, and especially because of the confusion that AI has created across those groups, that we really need new models — and models that are capable of being flexible.
But then, as everyone's talked about, how do you gain the skills and the judgment to really supervise the output?

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts that AI value depends on institutional redesign and human oversight, then materially develops the proposition through concrete proposals for internal associate upskilling, experiential learning and cross-institutional training partnerships. It also reinforces a copilot model in which subject-matter experts control AI use and lawyers must develop judgment to supervise outputs.
qs: And I said, for the next couple of years, it may be the case that you almost have to build an internal version of a law school to upskill your new associates sufficiently so that they're contributing value in the way that you expect them to.
And I think, to your point, it's probably a partnership across all of the areas that we talked about.

st.an: The source accepts that AI will accelerate redesign of the billable-hour production model while preserving a central role for lawyers who supervise AI output. It materially extends the synthesis by proposing internal upskilling, experiential learning and cross-sector partnerships to replace weakened associate apprenticeship pathways.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s human-led work-redesign proposition and materially develops its organisational and labour implications. It identifies the loss of junior work as a professional-development problem, argues that effective verification requires cultivated judgment, and proposes experiential training and cross-sector collaboration while noting firms’ capacity and incentive constraints.

st.t: AI writing: Present gains can weaken future judgment
st.an: Leonard supports selective, human-directed augmentation: she retains drafting as her own work while using AI for fact-checking, research, feedback and limited ideation. Her personal workflow aligns with preserving authorship and verification, though it does not provide evidence about long-term judgment or competence effects.
qs: If I was working in the book and there were things like numbers, or I wanted to make sure that I was saying something factually accurate, I would quickly run a search in Perplexity, which of course gives you the underlying resources themselves, and take those and make sure that I did it as a sort of fact-checking or deepening of some of the things I was exploring.

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central proposition that AI intensifies longstanding weaknesses in lawyer preparation and apprenticeship, requiring flexible, coordinated development across law schools, employers and continuing legal education providers. Its claims are largely framing and anecdotal rather than evidence of reform effectiveness.
qs: There is such a gap, especially in the handoff between schools and employers, and especially because of the confusion that AI has created across those groups, that we really need new models — and models that are capable of being flexible.

And as a legal education organization focusing on preparing lawyers for the future and for their current practice, it's really important for us to provide programming that's helpful and also partner with law schools and law firms to make sure people are ready.

st.t: Personalized coaching: Perceived follow-through lacks validated outcomes
st.an: The source directly supports the proposition that ongoing personal inputs can make general-purpose AI useful as an individualized coach and motivator. Its evidence remains first-hand perceptions of convenience, encouragement and guidance, with no validated health outcomes or legal-performance findings.
qs: I basically write in what I've eaten in the day, what exercise I've done, and I have it suggest what I should do, let's say, for lunch or for dinner.
Try this next tomorrow.”  So it's been both like a coach and motivator.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source directly supports practitioner-led redesign by arguing that AI plans succeed only through human buy-in and execution. Its adaptable implementation guidance, competency-building initiative and augmentation anecdotes reinforce experimentation and shared implementation, while offering no measured evidence of broader restructuring or outcomes.
qs: But unless you have human buy-in and human engagement, none of it actually works in the end.

You look at your own space and you say, “I love this idea, and this won't work for that reason.” But you literally lay out almost a blueprint of how you could incorporate some of the ideas that meet the most challenging issues that we've mentioned — intergenerational conflict, AI, and all those types of things.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source directly endorses proactive adaptation and capability-building before AI-driven disruption, aligning with the cluster’s engagement-first call for sustained learning rather than waiting for technological certainty. Its support is predictive and anecdotal, not evidence of implementation effectiveness.
qs: We have to be building new superpowers, or we could be obsolete.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source supports selective augmentation by presenting AI as an aid that can amplify and sharpen human work, while insisting that implementation depends on human buy-in, engagement and execution. It especially reinforces the cluster’s implementation point, but offers no measured evidence on productivity, verification costs or junior staffing effects.
qs: But unless you have human buy-in and human engagement, none of it actually works in the end.
So approaching something as enormous as a book project and knowing that I could amplify it and augment it and make it sharper was also confidence-building.

kp.k: AI transformation requires collective leadership and sustained implementation
kp.d: Leonard recommends that firm leaders establish a vision and environments for collective contribution rather than claim to possess all the answers. She describes transformation as continuous, messy and potentially involving departures, not a finite workshop exercise. Her recommendations are illustrated through a fictional firm retreat, not demonstrated organizational outcomes; human engagement remains necessary even when AI can generate implementation plans.
qs: Change and transformation are not about one person knowing how to do everything. It's about that person setting the vision for their time together, and then creating environments where everybody gets to contribute to change.
innovation, change management, and transformation happen continuously and forever.
But unless you have human buy-in and human engagement, none of it actually works in the end. And the implementation is the hardest part.

kp.k: Existing success and workload can impede organizational change
kp.d: Leonard's fictional characters, described as composites informed by consulting encounters and former students, illustrate different barriers to change: successful partners may prefer the status quo, while recently promoted partners face business development, caregiving, mentoring and succession responsibilities. These are practitioner observations and fictional illustrations, not quantified findings about firm populations.
qs: And a lot of the characters are composites of people that we meet in our travels.
And then there's the skeptic, who wants nothing to do with this because they're very successful in the world that exists today.

And then in the middle layer, you've got the partners who have recently become partners, are actively trying to build their books, are caretakers of parents and children, and expected to mentor down and also help the generation above them think about succession planning.

kp.k: Design thinking can strengthen client understanding
kp.d: Leonard presents design thinking as a way to develop empathy beyond the firm's internal perspective, particularly as lawyers approach partnership and face changed skill expectations. The book uses interviews with fictional external general counsel to surface client frustrations and preferences. Crane recommends adapting selected exercises to departments or client relationships rather than requiring adoption of an entire retreat format.
qs: And I think the design thinking methodology introduces that group to the concept of empathy.
When you've been in a law firm, you are sort of siloed, and you have a law firm perspective of the relationship.
And that's why we had, in the book, the outside general counsel who come in, and they are interviewed about the things that frustrate them and delight them about their firms.

kp.k: Historical firm models are contingent, not inevitable
kp.d: Leonard argues that the early-20th-century legal business system met its historical circumstances but need not govern modern firms. She attributes the rise of hourly billing to a consumer lawsuit seeking billing clarity and claims it unintentionally shifted lawyers toward corporate clients. The transcript supplies no case identification or supporting historical documentation; these are Leonard's historical assertions supporting redesign.
qs: I realized that the system, which emerged in the early 20th century, was a really great example of well-designed businesses. It really met the moment.

And then the rise of the billable hour was really not to benefit the firms. It was actually the outcome of a consumer lawsuit against law firms for the lack of clarity in the way that they would bill their services.
And it unintentionally gave rise to this system that slowly moved lawyers away from people and toward corporate clients.
And so the point is that none of this is how it has to be.

kp.k: Rate increases allegedly mask declining billable hours
kp.d: Leonard asserts that hours across the Am Law 200 peaked in 2003 and have declined steadily since, while higher rates have sustained the business model. She interprets this as underlying change that AI and other forces will accelerate. No dataset, measurement definition or supporting study is provided in the transcript.
qs: And then I mention in the book that the billable hour’s high watermark, in terms of numbers of hours across the Am Law 200, was really back in 2003, and it's been steadily declining ever since.
We're blind to that because the rates have gone up so much that it's remained a healthy business model.
But to me, it shows how much under the surface has already changed and will be accelerated by AI and other forces.

kp.d: Crane describes a longstanding gap between theoretical legal education and practice, historically bridged by apprenticeship subsidized by clients paying for first- and second-year associates. She argues that the importance of leverage has eroded one-to-one partner–associate learning. This is her diagnosis framing the training discussion, rather than a measured finding.
qs: the model of training, from theory in law school to practice under the Cravath model, with apprenticeship and clients subsidizing that training by paying for first and second years.
And the apprenticeship model, as leverage has gotten to be very important, has kind of fallen away from what it used to be: one-on-one partners and an associate learning from that person.

kp.k: AI intensifies the law-school-to-employer training gap
kp.d: Leonard calls for flexible new training models and unconventional partnerships because AI compounds an already problematic handoff between schools and employers. Recounting a conversation with a firm leader, she suggests firms may need something resembling internal law schools over the next couple of years, while emphasizing that firms lack both readiness and financial incentives for that role.
qs: There is such a gap, especially in the handoff between schools and employers, and especially because of the confusion that AI has created across those groups, that we really need new models — and models that are capable of being flexible.

for the next couple of years, it may be the case that you almost have to build an internal version of a law school to upskill your new associates sufficiently so that they're contributing value in the way that you expect them to.
And that's not anything that any law firm, A, is set up to do, nor is financially incentivized to do.

kp.k: Simulation may replace lost learning opportunities
kp.d: Crane identifies the unresolved problem of developing skills and judgment to supervise AI output when AI takes over current work. She reports interest in experimental, experiential and simulated learning, supported by collaboration among schools, firms, consultants, education organizations and in-house counsel. These are proposed directions, not evaluated training interventions.
qs: we're looking to do some more experimental and experiential and simulated learning so that people can do more practice.

Everyone's concerned about the current work being given to AI, as it probably should be. But then, as everyone's talked about, how do you gain the skills and the judgment to really supervise the output?
It's law schools and consultants and organizations like ours and the AAA and law firms and in-house counsel, to be honest.

kp.k: Routine junior work is not proven judgment formation
kp.d: McCormack challenges the assumption that routine work reliably produced sound judgment, arguing that training quality depended heavily on individual partners. She sees an opportunity for better-designed training and predicts new legal needs and more work for lawyers, but expressly acknowledges that optimism does not establish how the replacement system will operate.
qs: I'm not sure that doing grunt work really was what created great judgment to begin with.

Sometimes individual new lawyers got excellent training because they had an individual partner who really took an interest in them, and others had significantly less excellent experiences. It was not excellent across the board.
I think lawyers are going to have more to do
Just because I'm optimistic that we will work it out and it will make it better isn't a good answer to what it is going to look like necessarily.

kp.k: Junior outcomes depend on balancing automation and critical thinking
kp.d: McCormack frames the risk that business pressures encourage juniors to outsource thinking before developing expertise. Leonard uses two fictional associates, informed by contrasting attitudes she encounters in practice, to explore balancing technological enthusiasm with concern about critical thinking. She conditionally predicts better junior careers and greater retention if training is redesigned successfully, citing her own dissatisfaction with document review as personal experience rather than labor-market evidence.
qs: In your book, the junior associate, who is quite self-aware, is worried about how she's not going to learn what she feels like she wants to learn if she can outsource her thinking to AI.
I think we're going to retain a lot more lawyers in the profession.
And I had two junior associate characters: Priya, who is the self-aware one who's worried about the loss of her critical thinking skills, and Alex, who is all speed ahead with technology.
But overall, I'm very optimistic that if we do this right, the life of a junior lawyer will be much better than it has been in the past.

kp.k: Expert-controlled AI collaboration preserves human responsibility
kp.d: Leonard's account of writing the book illustrates augmentation rather than substitution: she retained drafting, used Perplexity to locate sources for factual checking, sought AI feedback on consistency and editing, and used AI-generated ideas specifically to illustrate divergent ideation. She also used reverse interviewing to stimulate her own thinking and argues that these tools currently work best with subject-matter experts able to reject unsuitable suggestions. Human researchers and editors also contributed.
qs: I thought about the spectrum of human-machine collaboration and what things I really wanted to keep mine alone. And for me, that was the drafting part.

I would quickly run a search in Perplexity, which of course gives you the underlying resources themselves, and take those and make sure that I did it as a sort of fact-checking or deepening of some of the things I was exploring.
So I did work with AI to come up with different ideas that I used in the book to show that part of it.
And as you both know, I think right now it works best for subject matter experts.
I was working alongside it, but in control of it the whole time.

kp.k: Cross-organizational collaboration supports adaptation at AI speed
kp.d: Crane argues that the pace of AI change exceeds any individual's or organization's capacity to keep up, making shared experimentation and learning from successes and failures important. She describes collaboration between PLI, AAA and Leonard's team around a Law Firm AI Strategy Program as an example, but offers no measured evidence of its effects on firms.
qs: we are all learning, and things are moving faster than any one person or any one organization can possibly stay on top of.

it's so much easier to collaborate and learn from each other's successes and failures, and help each other get to the point, because it's moving too quickly for any one person or organization to handle.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Jen Leonard predicts that AI will accelerate changes already occurring beneath law firms’ apparently healthy hourly-billing economics.
pts.d: Leonard argues that established law-firm arrangements are historically contingent rather than necessary features of legal practice. She links AI to the acceleration of underlying change, citing her claim that hours across the AmLaw 200 peaked in 2003 and have since declined while rate increases sustained the business model. She does not predict a specific replacement pricing model or a date when hourly billing will end.

pts.k: Sharon Crane says the pace of AI-era change exceeds what any individual or organisation can track alone, making collaboration an important means of adaptation.
pts.d: Crane presents partnerships and shared learning from experiments as a response to rapid change. Her examples concern collaboration among PLI, the American Arbitration Association and Creative Lawyers, including distribution of the Law Firm AI Strategy Program. This is an experience-based organisational claim, not a measured comparison of collaborative and independent adoption.

pts.k: Leonard says AI can generate organisational plans, but successful law-firm transformation still depends on human engagement and execution.
pts.d: Leonard distinguishes the production of ideas and implementation plans from their actual adoption. She describes transformation as continuous and potentially uncomfortable, rather than something completed through a short series of workshops. Her fictional retreat illustrates this argument; it is not evidence of an actual firm’s AI transformation results.

pts.k: Leonard presents AI as an augmentation tool for research, feedback, ideation and stimulating expert thinking, with the human remaining in control.
pts.d: Drawing on writing her book and the approach she teaches law-firm clients, Leonard describes retaining authorship of the draft while using AI for source discovery and fact-checking support, editorial feedback, consistency checks, divergent ideas and reverse interviewing. She qualifies the usefulness of this collaboration by saying AI currently works best for subject-matter experts who can reject suggestions that would not work in a law firm. This is a copilot account rather than a claim that AI should independently deliver legal advice.

pts.k: Leonard predicts that AI will disrupt the already problematic transition from law school to employment, potentially requiring firms to provide substantially more internal education.
pts.d: Leonard argues for flexible training models because AI is creating confusion about the capabilities employers need and the preparation graduates receive. She suggests that, for the next couple of years, firms may effectively need an internal law school to upskill new associates. She explicitly qualifies this proposal by noting that firms are neither set up nor financially incentivised to provide it, and calls for unusual partnerships instead of presenting internal training as an established solution.

pts.k: Crane identifies an unresolved training problem: delegating existing work to AI raises questions about how lawyers develop the skills and judgment to supervise its output.
pts.d: Crane expects more experimental, experiential and simulated learning and says PLI is looking to undertake more of it. She frames training for human supervision of AI output as an open problem requiring cooperation among law schools, consultants, education organisations, law firms and in-house counsel. She does not claim that simulation has already been shown to replace experience gained through practice.

pts.k: Leonard predicts better retention and a better junior-lawyer experience if firms successfully combine AI adoption with redesigned education.
pts.d: Leonard connects her optimism to reducing tedious work and using simulated education to help juniors become capable more quickly. Her supporting personal example is leaving practice because she did not want to spend her time reviewing bankers’ boxes for relevance. She also reports observing contrasting associate attitudes toward AI and suggests that cautious and enthusiastic juniors can learn from one another. The predicted retention benefit is not quantified and is explicitly conditional on implementation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence offered is professional experience, personal AI use and illustrative fiction; the market argument also includes an uncited historical quantitative assertion.
pts.d: Leonard draws on consulting with law firms, conversations with firm leaders, reports from former students now in practice, her own departure from practice and AI-assisted book development. Crane draws on leading PLI and collaborating on legal education. Leonard explicitly describes the fictional characters as composites, so their experiences should not be treated as independent cases. Her AmLaw 200 hours assertion supplies a historical basis for the acceleration argument, but the transcript provides no dataset, methodology or supporting citation. No benchmarks, measured productivity gains, retention estimates or comparative training outcomes are supplied. The discussion also promotes Leonard’s book, published by Crane’s organisation; Crane acknowledges that relationship.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The speakers describe present experimentation and near-term training disruption, while leaving longer-term market and retention predictions undated.
pts.d: Relative to the supplied 2026 source dating, Leonard’s internal-law-school suggestion concerns 'the next couple of years'; no exact calendar endpoint is given. Her expert-led collaboration qualification applies 'right now.' AI’s acceleration of market change, Crane’s expectation of more simulated learning and Leonard’s retention prediction have no fixed horizon. Better junior experiences depend on getting implementation right and providing effective education. Organisational gains depend on human buy-in, and the training model remains unresolved.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims primarily concern law-firm leaders and new associates, with linked changes for legal educators and in-house teams.
pts.d: Firm leaders face ongoing business-model adaptation, implementation work and possible additional training responsibilities without established financial incentives. Junior associates face changing work assignments and an unresolved need to develop judgment for supervising AI, alongside the possibility of more engaging careers and improved retention. Subject-matter experts are positioned to benefit from controlled AI collaboration. Law schools, PLI, AAA and consultants are prospective partners in developing new educational arrangements; in-house counsel are included as collaborators and teams needing upskilling. The specific economic assertion concerns the AmLaw 200, whereas the training arguments address law firms more generally. The source does not specify aggregate employment losses or access-to-justice effects.
